source_span: the price upgrade is "modest" despite his new assumption that shipping disruptions continue because OECD commercial oil inventories have so far barely drawn since the war began
source_chain: Markets are pricing a prolonged Mideast conflict into 2027 (Brent to $97, Mar-2027 >$100 odds up to 25%) therefore Goldman raises Brent/WTI forecasts $5 to $85/$80 for Dec-2026 therefore the raise stays modest, not a jump to Goldman's own $120 upside case, because OECD commercial stocks (the price-relevant category) have barely drawn (only 26mb of the 543mb global visible draw), leaving fair value at $79, $18 below market; invalidation: a faster Mideast output recovery or an OECD commercial-stock draw that stays absent keeps prices capped, while a stalemate/escalation with 2027 Gulf output 4mb/d below pre-war levels sends Brent above $120.
pulse_chain: Brent breaks $100 and the 6-month contract hits its highest since June because traders stop treating disruption as fading therefore banks disagree on what's priced in: Goldman raises Brent/WTI $5 to $85/$80 for Dec-2026 on disruption running into 2027 but calls it modest because only 26mb of the 543mb global stock draw came from OECD commercial tanks, leaving fair value at $79, $18 under market, while SocGen's probability-weighted $109 (vs $99 spot) and JPM's Kaneva stay more skeptical of upside; invalidation: fast OECD commercial draws kill the cheap-oil case, while continued Gulf export adaptation plus weak Chinese buying lets the premium bleed out.
why: The pulse reproduces Goldman's $5 forecast raise, its self-described 'modest' framing, the 26mb/543mb OECD-inventory reasoning, the $79/$18-under-market fair value, and the same upside/downside invalidation conditions (Gulf export recovery vs. faster OECD draws) in compressed form without reversing or reattributing any step.
